title: Satellites get a new type of armour

vocab.articleQuote: The smart money is on quite a few such failures being caused by collisions with space debris.
vocab.meaning: Debris is the scattered bits and pieces left behind when something breaks apart — snapped branches after a storm, or metal and glass after a crash. It is leftover junk, spread around, that nobody is keeping track of. In this article it means **space debris**: the dead satellites, spent rocket parts and flecks of paint still circling Earth after decades of launches.
examples: After the windstorm, the soccer field was covered in debris — leaves, snapped branches and somebody's blown-away lunch bag.
We had to sweep up every last bit of debris from the broken beaker before anyone walked near that table again.

vocab.articleQuote: In tests, they successfully stop aluminium projectiles the size of a pea that have been accelerated by a gas gun to 7.2km a second.
vocab.meaning: A projectile is an object that has been thrown, fired or launched and is now flying on its own — a pitched baseball, an arrow, a bullet. It shares a root with the word *project*, which once meant to throw forward. In this article the projectiles are the pea-sized aluminium pellets that engineers fire from a gas gun to copy what space junk does to a satellite.
examples: In science class we learned that a kicked football is a projectile: once your foot leaves it, only gravity and the air are still acting on it.
The catapult our team built launched a marshmallow projectile clear across the gym.

vocab.articleQuote: a shield incorporating a layer of this foam a little over 6mm thick could provide the same protection as a conventional Whipple shield of twice the weight
vocab.meaning: Conventional means the usual way — the standard version that people already use, as opposed to a new or unusual one. It is not praise and not an insult; it simply marks something as the familiar option. In this article a **conventional** Whipple shield is the ordinary two-layer aluminium design engineers have built for decades, and it is what every new material has to beat.
examples: The conventional way to open an essay is with a hook, but our teacher let us start with a list instead.
Our chess club sticks to conventional openings, so the other side usually knows what is coming.

concepts.name: Kinetic energy
concepts.articleQuote: Hurtling around Earth at roughly seven kilometres a second, even tiny pieces of debris pack quite a punch.
concepts.meaning:
A fleck of paint is harmless. You could catch one on your fingertip. But a fleck of paint in orbit can blast a crater in a satellite, and the only thing that changed is how fast it is moving.

Physicists call the energy stored in a moving object its **kinetic energy**, and the rule behind it is strange the first time you meet it. Double an object's mass and you double that energy. But double its *speed* and you multiply the energy by four. Ten times faster is a hundred times the energy. Speed counts for far more than size.

Picture two tennis balls. One rolls off a table and taps your shoe, and you barely feel it. The other comes off a serving machine at 100mph and hits your shoe, and you are limping to the nurse. Same ball, same mass — only the speed is different. Now push that ball to seven kilometres a second, the speed of junk in low orbit, which is about eight times the speed of a rifle bullet. At that speed it would not bruise a satellite. It would tear a hole straight through.

So when you want to know how much damage a moving object can do, ask how fast it is going before you ask how big it is.

concepts.name: Composite materials
concepts.articleQuote: One combines Kevlar, a fibre used to make bullet-proof jackets … with Nextel, a woven ceramic.
concepts.meaning:
Every material is a trade-off. Steel is strong but heavy. Plastic is light but soft. Ceramic is hard but shatters. For centuries, building something meant picking the least-bad single material for the job — until people began locking materials together instead.

Materials scientists call the result a **composite**: one material built from two or more different materials joined so the mixture does something neither could do alone. The word just means *put together from parts*. Usually one part is a stiff fibre and the other is a softer material that holds those fibres in place. Kevlar, the stuff in bullet-proof vests, is a mesh of extremely tough fibres. Nextel, its partner in this article, is ceramic drawn into threads and woven like cloth, which makes it hard in a way Kevlar is not. Bond the two and you get a sheet that is hard on the outside, tough on the inside, and still light enough to launch.

You already own composites. A bike helmet is stiff foam under a hard plastic shell. When your head hits the pavement, the shell spreads the force of the blow across a wide area instead of one point, and the foam crushes slowly underneath, which stretches the stop out over a longer time. Neither layer works by itself: bare foam tears open on a rock, and bare plastic passes the whole jolt through to your skull. Together they do the job, at a weight you can wear all afternoon without noticing.

That is the whole trick. When no single material has everything you need, build one that does.

quiz.question: Space debris is the leftover junk circling Earth — dead satellites, rocket parts, flecks of paint. Why can a piece no bigger than a pea seriously damage a working satellite?
options: It is made of a rare metal that dissolves aluminium on contact
It is travelling at roughly seven kilometres a second, so it carries enormous energy
It builds up an electric charge that short-circuits the satellite
It sticks to solar panels and blocks the sunlight they need
quiz.explanation: Speed, not size, is what makes orbital debris dangerous: at about seven kilometres a second even a tiny fragment carries a huge amount of kinetic energy.

quiz.question: In a Whipple shield, what does the outer bumper do to an incoming piece of debris?
options: It reflects the debris back out into space
It pulls the debris off course with a magnetic field
It breaks the debris into a spray of smaller, less energetic fragments
It melts the debris into a liquid that drains away
quiz.explanation: The bumper shatters the incoming object so that the main shield a few centimetres behind it only has to stop small, weaker fragments.

quiz.question: NASA found that a shield with a layer of aluminium foam "could provide the same protection as a conventional Whipple shield of twice the weight." What does conventional mean here?
options: Old-fashioned and no longer permitted in space
The usual, standard kind that engineers already build
Unusually cheap to manufacture
Designed by a convention of international scientists
quiz.explanation: Conventional marks the familiar, standard version of something — here, the ordinary two-layer aluminium shield the new foam is measured against.

quiz.question: Which of these is a projectile?
options: A pea-sized aluminium pellet fired from a gas gun
A roll of Kevlar fabric sitting in a factory
A wrench lying on an engineer's workbench
A ceramic tile bolted to the side of a spacecraft
quiz.explanation: A projectile is an object that has been thrown, fired or launched and is flying on its own — the other three are not moving at all.

quiz.question: What makes something a composite material?
options: It is a single pure material with nothing else added
It is any material light enough to be launched into orbit
It is a material that has been melted down and recycled
It is two or more different materials locked together so the mixture does what neither could do alone
quiz.explanation: A composite joins different materials — like tough Kevlar fibres with hard woven ceramic — so the combination beats either material on its own.
